name: Grace Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a fit-out crew for a subcontractor that does the insides of offices, shops and the odd dentist's surgery. Metal stud walls, plasterboard, suspended ceilings, doors, the lot, usually in buildings where the shell's done and we turn a concrete box into somewhere people work. I like the puzzle of it, getting eight trades through one floor without anyone tripping over each other. What wears me out is the hours when a shop has to open on a Monday and it's Friday and the ceiling grid's still on a pallet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly. I photograph the drawings and ask an AI to flag clashes, like a door that opens into a fire hose cabinet, and it catches about half of them before we get there. I use it to rework the programme when deliveries slip. Last spring we hired a little layout robot that drives round the floor and prints the wall lines in ink straight off the drawing, and I loved it, it did in a morning what takes two of us a day with a chalk line.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Owen works nights at the big distribution warehouse out by the ring road, so we pass each other at the door most days. Mei's thirteen and Ollie's ten. Mortgage on a new-build on the Larch Park estate, which I'd point out we didn't build, and honestly we've got less than a month put by, because my firm pays below the going rate and there's not much else round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit gutted, because the tools I use are good and I wanted more of them. At work I'd tell people to keep using what works. Online I'd probably just share a video of the layout robot and say this bit was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I stay where I am, good at my job, underpaid, in a town with few firms. The tools save me time, but the company pockets most of it. Nothing gets worse, nothing gets better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the AI for drawings and programmes, push my boss to hire the layout robot on every job because it pays for itself. I'd keep my eye out for a better-paid job with a firm that uses more of this stuff. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mildly bored by the idea, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a better-paid job. Is that likely round here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, there are maybe two other fit-out firms within an hour. I'm the best setter-out in this town and I'm paid like I'm still learning, because where else am I going to go? That's the deal in a small place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Owen use any of this in the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse is full of it already, scanners that tell him where to walk and what to pick. He jokes he's the robot's legs. It's the bit I worry about more than mine.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit gutted because the tools are good and I wanted more of them. I'd share a video of the layout robot online as the part that was real.
S0.think: I think I'd stay where I am: good at my job, underpaid, in a town with few firms. The company keeps most of the time the tools save.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for drawings and programmes and pushes her boss to hire the layout robot on every job. Watches for better-paid work with a firm using more technology.
S0.feel: Calm, a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: I'm the best setter-out in this town and I'm paid like I'm still learning, because where else am I going to go?
S0.fieldNote: Grace is an enthusiastic early user of AI and site robots, and the plateau disappoints her. Her limit isn't skill but a small local market that keeps her pay low. She's already more worried about her partner's warehouse job than her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people like me can get ahead if we're quick. At work I'd be the one showing the crew how to use the new kit. Online I'd post the useful stuff and ignore the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Interiors are fiddly and every building's a bit different, so the robots help rather than replace for a while. The person who can run the robots and read the drawings becomes the most useful one on site, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my boss to buy a layout robot outright and make me responsible for it. I'd do an online course on building information modelling, that's the 3D computer drawings everything is going to run off. I'd think about doing the same for Owen, getting him trained on the warehouse systems rather than just following them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Excited, honestly, with a little voice saying be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the little voice say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It says, you're excited because you think you'll be the one holding the remote. Everyone who gets excited about robots thinks they'll be the one holding the remote. Not everyone will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terry, who's been hanging doors for thirty years and is the best I've seen. He doesn't want a phone that does more than ring. I'd make sure he was the one checking the robot's doors, because nobody spots a bad hang like him.

S1.say: I'd say this is where people like me can get ahead if we're quick. I'd show my crew the new kit and post useful tips online.
S1.think: I think it's good for me because fiddly interiors mean robots help rather than replace for a while. Someone who runs robots and reads drawings becomes the most useful person on site.
S1.do: Asks her boss to buy a layout robot and put her in charge of it. Takes an online course in 3D building models and looks at training for Owen on warehouse systems.
S1.feel: Excited, with a small warning voice telling her to be careful.
S1.quote: Everyone who gets excited about robots thinks they'll be the one holding the remote.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption fits Grace's strengths and she leans in quickly. She is self-aware that early adopters all assume they'll be in control. She plans a role for her older colleague rather than writing him off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's work out who gets what instead of pretending we can stop it. I'd tell the crew to learn everything they can, fast. Online I'd try to be useful, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd say out loud. I can learn quick, but two years isn't long enough to save anything, and Owen's warehouse would be one of the first places to go fully automatic. Our two incomes are both in the firing line, and the second one is the more exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cut the things we can live without, the gym, the takeaways, the extra phone data. I'd go to the bigger fit-out firms in the city and offer myself as the person who sets up and runs their robots, even if it means an hour's drive. I'd push Owen to apply for the maintenance team at the warehouse, the people who fix the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, but busy. I'd be making lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drive an hour. What would that cost the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fuel, mainly, and me not being home for breakfast. With Owen on nights, somebody has to get the kids to school. We'd become a family that only ever meets in the hallway, and I'd tell myself it's temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound like you'd still be in control. Is that how it feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I've got skills a robot company would want for a while. But less than a month of money is less than a month of money. If both of us lost work in the same quarter, being clever wouldn't pay the mortgage.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening, so people should work out who gets what instead of trying to stop it. I'd tell my crew to learn everything fast and try to be useful online.
S2.think: I think it worries me more than I'd admit, because two years is too short to save and Owen's warehouse job is even more exposed than mine. Both our incomes are in the firing line.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, takeaways and phone extras in the first month. Offers herself to bigger city fit-out firms as a robot operator despite the commute and pushes Owen towards the warehouse maintenance team.
S2.feel: Tight in the chest but busy, making lists.
S2.quote: We'd become a family that only ever meets in the hallway, and I'd tell myself it's temporary.
S2.fieldNote: Grace feels in control because her skills are in demand, but she knows thin savings and her partner's exposure limit her. She doesn't blame anyone and focuses on who gets what. The cost she names is family time, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up, so use it. At work I'd push the firm to buy the kit early, while there's still a gap to win jobs. I'd post about what's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels doable for me. I'd have time to become the person a firm can't do without during the changeover, and build a bit of savings. After 2031, I honestly don't know, nobody does, but I'd be better placed than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the 3D modelling course and get a robotics certificate, there are short ones now for site machines. I'd start a little side business setting up layout robots for other small firms on weekends. Owen would retrain in machine maintenance by year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Like the night before a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side business look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, a hired layout robot and a van, going to small builders who can't justify owning one. I'd charge by the floor. I'd be renting out a robot that does my old job, and charging for the bit only I can do, which is knowing when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said after 2031 you don't know. What's your best guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My best guess is the robots get good enough that they don't need me to check them either. By then I'd want some money in the bank and Owen in a job that's about people or machines. Past that, I'm not going to pretend.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a good run-up to be used well. I'd push the firm to buy kit early while there's still an advantage to win.
S3.think: I think five years is doable, giving me time to become indispensable in the changeover and build some savings. After 2031 nobody knows, but I'd be better placed than most.
S3.do: Finishes a 3D modelling course and a short robotics certificate in the first year. Starts a weekend side business setting up layout robots for small builders and gets Owen retrained in machine maintenance.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a positive way, like the night before a new job.
S3.quote: I'd be renting out a robot that does my old job, and charging for the bit only I can do, which is knowing when it's wrong.
S3.fieldNote: Five years plays to Grace's strengths: she builds a side business around the robot that replaces her old task. She's candid that she can't see past the arrival date. Her household plan includes moving Owen out of the most exposed role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and anyone who doesn't plan now will regret it. At work I'd tell the younger ones to treat this as their main career skill. I'd be optimistic out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years worries me in a different way, because it's long enough to get comfortable. I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, and probably running something to do with robots on sites. Then the robots run themselves and I'm fifty-three with a skill that's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the side business slowly, putting a bit of the profit into a second-hand layout robot of my own by year three or four. I'd save for the kids' studies and talk Mei out of anything too easy to automate, gently. I'd keep learning every year, because the tools will keep changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Hopeful, mostly, with a question at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mei want to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be an architect, which I think is great. I'd tell her to be the architect who's out on site, not the one who only draws. The drawing part is what the computer is already best at, it's the muddy boots part that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years could make you comfortable. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set myself a check every year, my birthday, say. Ask, is this still needed, and what's next. Owen would laugh at me making a spreadsheet of my own career, but that's me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and anyone who doesn't plan now will regret it. I'd tell younger workers to treat this as their main career skill.
S4.think: I think ten years is long enough to get comfortable running robots on sites. Then they could run themselves and I'd be fifty-three with a skill that's finished.
S4.do: Grows her side business and buys a second-hand layout robot by year three or four. Saves for her children's studies, guides her daughter's course choice, and keeps retraining each year.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, with an open question at the end.
S4.quote: The drawing part is what the computer is already best at, it's the muddy boots part that lasts.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Grace's risk is complacency rather than speed, and she plans a yearly check on herself. She'd invest in her own machine once the side business pays. Her advice to her daughter favours on-site, hands-on roles over desk work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Owen more than me. What would help is support for people in jobs like his to retrain before they're let go, not after, and a bit of breathing room on mortgages while families switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what happens to the people who were best at the old way. Terry can hang a door so it closes with one finger, and in ten years nobody will care. That makes me sadder than the money.

headlineQuote: Terry can hang a door so it closes with one finger, and in ten years nobody will care.
portrait: Grace Zhang is a 43-year-old crew lead for a fit-out subcontractor that builds the insides of offices and shops, with two kids, a partner on warehouse night shifts, a mortgage and less than a month saved. She uses AI every day and loved a layout robot she tried. The plateau bores her, and steady disruption looks like her chance to become the one who runs the robots. AGI in two years makes her anxious, mostly because her partner's job is more exposed than hers. With five or ten years she plans a weekend business renting out layout robots, retraining for her partner and a yearly check on her own skills.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mainly because her partner's warehouse job would go first and they'd have no time to save.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining for workers in exposed jobs before they're let go, and breathing room on mortgages while families switch.
